# TrustPlane

> TrustPlane is an open-source **auth plane**: request-bound authorization for AI agents, machine callers, service APIs, and MCP/tool servers. Instead of presenting a long-lived API key or bearer token, a caller signs a **request proof** for one specific call — a canonical transcript signature over method, path, body hash, time bucket, nonce, and client identity — and the auth plane verifies it in the request path, before the request reaches the upstream API. In one line: SPIFFE authenticates workloads; TrustPlane authorizes requests.

TrustPlane is built for security, platform, and infrastructure teams shipping agentic and machine-to-machine workflows that should not depend on broad, long-lived machine credentials. It is open source, runs in your own infrastructure, and needs no hosted account or external dependency per request.

## Category
- Open-source machine authorization, AI agent authorization, MCP / tool-server authorization, service-to-service (machine-to-machine) authorization, non-human identity authorization, API-key alternative, request-bound authorization.

## Canonical terminology
Use these terms; they match the product and the documentation.
- **auth plane** (product name **TrustPlane Auth**) — verifies requests in the request path, in your infrastructure.
- **control plane** (product name **TrustPlane Control**) — manages trust anchors, enrollment, signed policy distribution, revocation, and audit. Not "governance plane".
- **provider-owned boundary** / **provider adapter** — the enforcement point the API owner deploys.
- **caller** — an agent or service making a call. Once enrolled it is a **client**, with a **client record**.
- **request proof** — a canonical transcript signature over method, path, body hash, time bucket, nonce, and client identity.
- **short-lived downstream JWT** (ES256) — minted after an allow, for boundary-to-upstream forwarding or backend verification.
- **enrolled public keys** and **trust anchors** — what makes enrollment work. Not "trust material".
- **evidence-grade audit** — a record per authorization decision.

## Two guarantees that are often confused
- **Request binding** stops a proof being reused against a *different* call. Change the method, path, or body and verification fails with `request_binding_mismatch`.
- **Replay protection** stops the *same* call being submitted twice, via nonce storage and time-bucket validation. It fails with `jti_replay`.

## What TrustPlane is
- An auth plane that verifies a request proof before a request reaches a protected API, then mints a short-lived downstream JWT.
- Something you run yourself: a reverse-proxy provider adapter in front of an existing API, Go library middleware, or a local broker plus sidecar. Enforcement happens in your own infrastructure.
- A signed trust-and-policy bundle model for route and source authorization, with replay protection so a proof is not accepted twice.
- Complementary to the identity you already have: SPIFFE/SPIRE, OIDC/JWT, or a local issuer.

## What TrustPlane is not
- Not API-key management: it does not rotate or hide a reusable shared secret; it verifies a fresh proof for each request.
- Not bearer-only OAuth ingress, and not generic IAM: the protected application still owns tenant, role, entitlement, and resource decisions.
- Not a SPIFFE replacement or a SPIFFE-only wrapper, not a service mesh, not a CA replacement, not a secrets manager.

## How it works
1. A caller already has a workload identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE, an OIDC/JWT issuer, or a local TrustPlane issuer).
2. It enrolls a public key against a trust anchor. The private key stays with the caller; TrustPlane holds only the public key and its expiry.
3. For each call, the SDK or CLI signs a request proof: a canonical transcript signature over method, path, body hash, time bucket, nonce, and client identity.
4. The auth plane verifies the signature, request binding, key and session state, replay protection, and policy. On allow it mints a short-lived ES256 downstream JWT and records an audit record. A stolen proof is close to worthless: it expires in seconds, covers exactly one request, and is refused a second time.

## Ways to deploy it
- **Provider adapter** — a reverse-proxy verifier in front of an unmodified upstream API; upstream code does not change.
- **Library middleware** — verify inside your own Go HTTP service.
- **Broker and sidecar** — a local broker signs request proofs; on Kubernetes it can require SPIFFE/SPIRE attested workload identity.

## Project status and where to get it
- TrustPlane is in public preview.
- Caller SDKs: Go and TypeScript/Node.js are available. A Python SDK is planned and not yet released.
- Source, SDKs, and examples: https://github.com/trustplane-dev
- Documentation: https://docs.auth.trustplane.dev
- Pricing: https://trustplane.dev/pricing.md — the open-source auth plane is $0, MIT licensed, self-hosted, with no usage limits.
- Managed fleet governance (signing, distribution, revocation, and audit at scale across many deployments) is a separate future direction. It is not part of the open-source project and is not for sale today.

## Pages
- [Home](https://trustplane.dev/): what request-bound authorization is, the problem with long-lived machine credentials, how it works, use cases, and FAQ.
- [TrustPlane Auth](https://trustplane.dev/auth.html): the auth plane — request proofs, request binding, replay protection, key and session state, signed bundles, downstream JWT issuance, adapter and broker deployment, audit.
- [TrustPlane Control](https://trustplane.dev/control.html): the control plane — trust anchors, enrollment, signed policy distribution, revocation, audit, multitenant fleets, RBAC.
- [Solutions](https://trustplane.dev/solutions.html): AI agents, MCP and tool servers, service-to-service APIs, and partner machine clients.
- [Pricing](https://trustplane.dev/pricing.html): the open-source project is free; managed fleet governance is a future direction.
- [Downloads](https://trustplane.dev/downloads.html): CLI, Helm chart, container images, SDKs, and how to evaluate the auth plane in front of one API.
- [Documentation](https://docs.auth.trustplane.dev): setup and integration guidance.

## SDKs
- [Go SDK](https://github.com/trustplane-dev/trustplane-auth-sdk-go): sign request proofs from Go services and agents.
- [TypeScript SDK](https://github.com/trustplane-dev/trustplane-auth-sdk-js): sign request proofs from Node.js and TypeScript runtimes.
- Python SDK: planned, not yet released.

## Common questions this site answers
- How do you authorize AI agents that call APIs and tools?
- How is request-bound authorization different from API keys and OAuth bearer tokens?
- What is the difference between request binding and replay protection?
- What is the difference between the auth plane and the control plane?
- Is TrustPlane an identity provider?
- Where does enforcement happen?
- What is a secure alternative to API keys for machine-to-machine access?
- How do you authorize MCP / tool-server calls?
- How do you stop stolen or replayed machine credentials?
- How do you add request-level authorization in front of an existing API without rewriting it?
- How do you authorize non-human identities such as agents, services, and workloads?
- Does TrustPlane replace OAuth, IAM, or a service mesh?
- Do I need Kubernetes or a hosted service to run it?
- Does it work with SPIFFE, OIDC, and MCP?
